questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Detection of extra elements: nitrogen, sulphur and halogens
questions.question: In Lassaigne's test, the sodium fusion extract is boiled with $FeSO_4$, acidified and then treated with $Fe^{3+}$. A Prussian blue colour is obtained. This confirms the presence of

solution.key_concept: During sodium fusion, nitrogen is converted to $NaCN$. This $NaCN$ finally gives Prussian blue $Fe_4[Fe(CN)_6]_3$.
steps: During fusion, nitrogen forms $NaCN$: $Na + C + N \rightarrow NaCN$.
Boiling with $FeSO_4$ gives $Na_4[Fe(CN)_6]$.
Acidifying and adding $Fe^{3+}$ gives Prussian blue $Fe_4[Fe(CN)_6]_3$.
solution.why_not_others: Sulphur gives a violet colour with sodium nitroprusside. Chlorine gives a white $AgCl$ precipitate. When N and S are both present, a blood-red colour forms with $Fe^{3+}$, not Prussian blue.
solution.common_trap: Confusing the blood-red test for N and S together with the Prussian blue test for N alone.
solution.time_saving_tip: Prussian blue contains cyanide, and cyanide comes from nitrogen.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Detection of extra elements: nitrogen, sulphur and halogens
questions.question: Before testing for halogens with $AgNO_3$, the sodium fusion extract is boiled with dilute $HNO_3$. The purpose of this step is to
options: Decompose $NaCN$ and $Na_2S$, which would otherwise interfere with the test
Convert the sodium halide into the free halogen
Oxidise $Fe^{2+}$ to $Fe^{3+}$ for the Prussian blue test

solution.key_concept: $NaCN$ and $Na_2S$ also react with $AgNO_3$. They must therefore be destroyed before the halide test is done.
steps: The extract may contain $NaCN$ and $Na_2S$ along with $NaX$.
These would give precipitates with $AgNO_3$ and mask the result.
Boiling with $HNO_3$ destroys them, so only the silver halide precipitates.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): Decompose $NaCN$ and $Na_2S$, which would otherwise interfere with the test
solution.why_not_others: The halide must stay as $X^-$ to react with $Ag^+$. $PbS$ forms only with lead acetate. The Prussian blue test is a separate test for nitrogen.
solution.common_trap: Thinking $HNO_3$ is added only to acidify the solution, without seeing why the interfering ions must be removed.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Detection of extra elements: nitrogen, sulphur and halogens
questions.question: The sodium fusion extract of an organic compound gives a blood-red colour with $Fe^{3+}$ ions. The species responsible for this colour is

solution.key_concept: When N and S are both present, $NaSCN$ forms. It gives blood-red $[Fe(SCN)]^{2+}$ with $Fe^{3+}$.
steps: N and S together form $NaSCN$ during fusion.
The reaction is $NaSCN + Fe^{3+} \rightarrow [Fe(SCN)]^{2+}$, which is blood red.
solution.why_not_others: $Fe_4[Fe(CN)_6]_3$ is Prussian blue, the test for N. $Na_4[Fe(CN)_5NOS]$ is the violet product in the test for S. $PbS$ is a black precipitate.
solution.common_trap: Matching the colour to the Prussian blue complex just because $Fe^{3+}$ is used in both tests.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Detection of extra elements: nitrogen, sulphur and halogens
questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: Hydrazine ($N_2H_4$) does not give Lassaigne's test for nitrogen.
statements.R: Hydrazine contains no carbon, so $CN^-$ cannot form during sodium fusion.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: The Lassaigne test for N depends on forming $NaCN$, and this needs both carbon and nitrogen.
steps: The fusion reaction is $Na + C + N \rightarrow NaCN$.
Hydrazine has nitrogen but no carbon.
No $NaCN$ forms, so no Prussian blue appears. R therefore explains A.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
solution.why_not_others: Both statements are factually true, and R gives the direct cause of A.
solution.common_trap: Assuming that any compound containing nitrogen will give the Lassaigne test.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Detection of extra elements: nitrogen, sulphur and halogens
questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: The violet colour obtained when the sodium fusion extract is treated with sodium nitroprusside is due to $Na_4[Fe(CN)_5NOS]$.
statements.II: A yellow precipitate obtained with $AgNO_3$ that is insoluble in $NH_4OH$ indicates iodine.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: This question tests the products and colours of the sulphur and halogen tests.
steps: The sulphur test is $Na_2S + Na_2[Fe(CN)_5NO] \rightarrow Na_4[Fe(CN)_5NOS]$, which is violet. Statement I is correct.
$AgI$ is yellow and insoluble in $NH_4OH$. Statement II is correct.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
solution.why_not_others: Both statements agree with the standard observations, so no option that marks either one incorrect can be right.
solution.common_trap: Confusing pale yellow $AgBr$, which is sparingly soluble, with yellow $AgI$, which is insoluble.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Detection of functional groups: hydroxyl, carbonyl, carboxyl and amino
questions.question: Which reagent gives a violet colour with phenol but does not respond to alcohols?

solution.key_concept: Phenolic $-OH$ gives a violet colour with neutral $FeCl_3$; alcohols do not respond.
steps: Phenol reacts with neutral $FeCl_3$ to give a violet colour.
Alcohols give no such colour.
solution.why_not_others: Lucas reagent is used to classify alcohols. Tollens' reagent tests for aldehydes. 2,4-DNP tests for carbonyl compounds.
solution.common_trap: Choosing Lucas reagent just because it is linked with the $-OH$ group.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Detection of functional groups: hydroxyl, carbonyl, carboxyl and amino
questions.question: Which of the following alcohols produces turbidity with Lucas reagent in about 5 minutes at room temperature?

solution.key_concept: With Lucas reagent, 3° alcohols give turbidity immediately, 2° alcohols in about 5 minutes, and 1° alcohols not at room temperature.
steps: Propan-2-ol, $CH_3CH(OH)CH_3$, is a secondary alcohol.
Secondary alcohols give turbidity in about 5 minutes.
solution.why_not_others: 2-Methylpropan-2-ol is 3° and gives turbidity immediately. Ethanol and methanol are 1° and give no turbidity at room temperature.
solution.common_trap: Mixing up the response times of 2° and 3° alcohols.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Detection of functional groups: hydroxyl, carbonyl, carboxyl and amino
questions.question: Benzoic acid and phenol can be distinguished from each other by treating them with

solution.key_concept: A carboxylic acid releases $CO_2$ with $NaHCO_3$, but phenol is too weak an acid to react.
steps: The reaction is $RCOOH + NaHCO_3 \rightarrow RCOONa + H_2O + CO_2$, which gives brisk effervescence.
Phenol gives no effervescence, so the two compounds are distinguished.
solution.why_not_others: Lucas reagent is for alcohols. 2,4-DNP is for carbonyl compounds. Tollens' reagent is for aldehydes. None of these separates benzoic acid from phenol.
solution.common_trap: Assuming phenol also releases $CO_2$ because it is acidic.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Detection of functional groups: hydroxyl, carbonyl, carboxyl and amino
questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_I.label: A
list_I.text: Ceric ammonium nitrate test on an alcohol

list_I.label: B
list_I.text: Schiff's reagent test on an aldehyde

list_I.label: D
list_I.text: Azo dye test on an aromatic primary amine

solution.key_concept: Each functional-group test gives its own characteristic observation.
steps: Ceric ammonium nitrate gives a red colour with an alcohol: A-IV.
Schiff's reagent gives a pink colour with an aldehyde: B-III.
2,4-DNP gives a yellow-orange precipitate with a ketone: C-I.
The azo dye test gives an orange-red dye: D-II.
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) swaps the alcohol and aldehyde results. Option (2) swaps the results of B and C. Option (3) swaps the results of A and D.
solution.common_trap: Confusing the red colour of the ceric ammonium nitrate test with the orange-red azo dye.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Detection of functional groups: hydroxyl, carbonyl, carboxyl and amino
questions.question: Which of the following statements about tests for functional groups are correct?

statements.A: Benzaldehyde gives a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent but does not give a red precipitate with Fehling's solution.
statements.B: The carbylamine test is given by both primary and secondary amines.
statements.C: Acetone gives a red colour with sodium nitroprusside in alkaline medium.
statements.D: Phenol gives a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol with bromine water.
statements.E: Phenol gives brisk effervescence of $CO_2$ with $NaHCO_3$.

solution.key_concept: This question tests the scope of the aldehyde, methyl ketone, amine and phenol tests.
steps: A is correct: the Fehling's test works only for aliphatic aldehydes.
B is incorrect: only primary amines give the carbylamine test.
C is correct: methyl ketones give a red colour with alkaline sodium nitroprusside.
D is correct.
E is incorrect: phenol is too weak an acid to react with $NaHCO_3$.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): A, C and D only
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) includes B, which is false. Option (3) includes E, which is false. Option (4) leaves out D, which is true.
solution.common_trap: Thinking secondary amines also give the isocyanide smell.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Preparation of inorganic compounds: Mohr's salt and potash alum
questions.question: The number of water molecules of crystallisation in one formula unit of Mohr's salt is

solution.key_concept: The formula of Mohr's salt is $FeSO_4\cdot(NH_4)_2SO_4\cdot6H_2O$.
steps: Reading the formula, there are 6 water molecules per formula unit.
solution.why_not_others: 7 is the number in $FeSO_4\cdot7H_2O$, green vitriol. 12 and 24 belong to potash alum, as $KAl(SO_4)_2\cdot12H_2O$ and $K_2SO_4\cdot Al_2(SO_4)_3\cdot24H_2O$.
solution.common_trap: Recalling the hydrate count of ferrous sulphate or of alum instead.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Preparation of inorganic compounds: Mohr's salt and potash alum
questions.question: In the preparation of Mohr's salt, a little dilute $H_2SO_4$ is added to the water used to dissolve ferrous sulphate and ammonium sulphate. This is done to
options: Precipitate the ammonium ions as ammonium bisulphate

solution.key_concept: Acid is added to suppress the hydrolysis of the metal ions.
steps: $Fe^{2+}$ undergoes hydrolysis in water.
Adding dilute $H_2SO_4$ suppresses this hydrolysis, so pure crystals can form.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): Suppress the hydrolysis of $Fe^{2+}$ ions
solution.why_not_others: Oxidation to $Fe^{3+}$ is unwanted, because it makes the product yellowish. The water of crystallisation must stay in the crystals. No ammonium precipitate is formed.
solution.common_trap: Assuming the acid acts as an oxidant or a dehydrating agent.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Preparation of inorganic compounds: Mohr's salt and potash alum
questions.question: How many moles of $SO_4^{2-}$ ions are present in 94.8 g of potash alum, $K_2SO_4\cdot Al_2(SO_4)_3\cdot24H_2O$ (molar mass 948 g/mol)?

solution.key_concept: One formula unit $K_2SO_4\cdot Al_2(SO_4)_3\cdot24H_2O$ contains 4 sulphate ions.
steps: Moles of alum = 94.8 / 948 = 0.1 mol.
Each unit has 1 + 3 = 4 $SO_4^{2-}$ ions.
solution.why_not_others: 0.1 mol is the number of moles of alum, not of sulphate. 0.2 mol assumes only 2 sulphates per 948 g unit. 0.8 mol uses 474 g/mol together with 4 sulphates.
solution.common_trap: Mixing the two formula units: 474 g/mol goes with 2 sulphates and 948 g/mol goes with 4.
solution.time_saving_tip: Either unit works: 94.8/474 × 2 also gives 0.4 mol.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Preparation of inorganic compounds: Mohr's salt and potash alum
questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: Prolonged heating of the solution is avoided during the preparation of Mohr's salt.
statements.R: Prolonged heating oxidises $Fe^{2+}$ to $Fe^{3+}$, which makes the product yellowish.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: Pale green $Fe^{2+}$ must be protected from oxidation during the preparation.
steps: The solution is concentrated only by gentle heating.
Prolonged heating converts $Fe^{2+}$ to $Fe^{3+}$, which gives a yellowish product.
R is the reason for A.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
solution.why_not_others: Both statements are true, and R directly explains A.
solution.common_trap: Thinking heating is avoided only to protect the water of crystallisation.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Preparation of inorganic compounds: Mohr's salt and potash alum
questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: Potash alum is a double salt, and in aqueous solution it gives $K^+$, $Al^{3+}$ and $SO_4^{2-}$ ions in the ratio 1:1:2.
statements.II: Mohr's salt is used as a primary standard in redox titrations because the $Fe^{2+}$ in it is stable to air oxidation.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: Double salts dissociate completely into their constituent ions, and the $Fe^{2+}$ in Mohr's salt is stable in air.
steps: In $KAl(SO_4)_2\cdot12H_2O$, $K^+:Al^{3+}:SO_4^{2-} = 1:1:2$, and all these ions are released in water. Statement I is correct.
The $Fe^{2+}$ in Mohr's salt resists air oxidation, which makes it a primary standard. Statement II is correct.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
solution.why_not_others: Neither statement contains an error.
solution.common_trap: Taking the ion ratio from the $K_2SO_4\cdot Al_2(SO_4)_3$ formula as 2:2:4 and judging it different from 1:1:2. The two ratios are the same.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Preparation of organic compounds: acetanilide, p-nitroacetanilide, aniline yellow and iodoform
questions.question: Aniline yellow, prepared by coupling benzenediazonium chloride with aniline, is chemically

solution.key_concept: Aniline yellow is p-aminoazobenzene, $C_6H_5N=NC_6H_4NH_2$.
steps: The coupling reaction is $C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^- + C_6H_5NH_2 \rightarrow p\text{-}H_2NC_6H_4N=NC_6H_5 + HCl$.
The product is p-aminoazobenzene.
solution.why_not_others: Benzenediazonium chloride is the reactant. Acetanilide is the acetylation product of aniline. p-Nitroaniline contains no azo group.
solution.common_trap: Naming the diazonium intermediate instead of the coupled product.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Preparation of organic compounds: acetanilide, p-nitroacetanilide, aniline yellow and iodoform
questions.question: In the preparation of p-nitroacetanilide, aniline is first converted to acetanilide and only then nitrated. The main reason for this is that acetylation
options: Makes the ring more strongly activated towards nitration
Directs the nitro group mainly to the meta position
Makes the compound highly soluble in the nitrating mixture
Moderates the activating effect of $-NH_2$ and protects it from oxidation

solution.key_concept: $-NHCOCH_3$ is moderately activating, whereas $-NH_2$ is strongly activating and easily oxidised.
steps: Direct nitration of aniline causes oxidation and over-substitution.
Acetylation gives the moderately activating $-NHCOCH_3$ group and protects nitrogen from oxidation.
Steric hindrance at the ortho positions then favours para substitution.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): Moderates the activating effect of $-NH_2$ and protects it from oxidation
solution.why_not_others: Acetylation reduces activation rather than increasing it. The $-NHCOCH_3$ group directs ortho/para, mainly para, not meta. Solubility is not the reason.
solution.common_trap: Thinking acetylation increases activation or changes the directing effect to meta.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Preparation of organic compounds: acetanilide, p-nitroacetanilide, aniline yellow and iodoform
questions.question: Which of the following compounds gives yellow crystals of iodoform when warmed with $I_2$ and $NaOH$?

solution.key_concept: The iodoform reaction is given by compounds that contain $CH_3CO-$ or $CH_3CH(OH)-$.
steps: Propan-2-ol, $CH_3CH(OH)CH_3$, contains the $CH_3CH(OH)-$ unit.
It therefore gives $CHI_3$.
solution.why_not_others: Methanol and propan-1-ol lack the $CH_3CH(OH)-$ unit. Pentan-3-one, $C_2H_5COC_2H_5$, has no $CH_3CO-$ group.
solution.common_trap: Assuming every ketone or every alcohol gives the iodoform test.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Preparation of organic compounds: acetanilide, p-nitroacetanilide, aniline yellow and iodoform
questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_II.label: I
list_II.text: Yellow crystals with an antiseptic smell, m.p. about 119 °C

list_II.label: III
list_II.text: Formed by coupling a diazonium salt with aniline

solution.key_concept: This question tests the characteristic appearance, melting point or method of preparation of each product.
steps: Acetanilide forms white crystals with m.p. about 114 °C: A-II.
p-Nitroacetanilide forms pale yellow crystals with m.p. about 214 °C: B-IV.
Aniline yellow is formed by diazo coupling: C-III.
Iodoform forms yellow crystals with m.p. about 119 °C and an antiseptic smell: D-I.
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) swaps the melting points of acetanilide (114 °C) and iodoform (119 °C). Option (3) swaps iodoform and p-nitroacetanilide. Option (4) swaps acetanilide and p-nitroacetanilide.
solution.common_trap: Confusing the close melting points 114 °C and 119 °C.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Preparation of organic compounds: acetanilide, p-nitroacetanilide, aniline yellow and iodoform
questions.question: Which of the following statements about the preparation of organic compounds are correct?

statements.A: Nitration of acetanilide is carried out below 10 °C to avoid polynitration and oxidation.
statements.B: o-Nitroacetanilide crystallises out from ethanol, while the p-isomer remains in the filtrate.
statements.C: Diazotisation of aniline is done at 0-5 °C because diazonium salts decompose at higher temperatures.
statements.D: Iodoform can be prepared from acetone using $KI$ and $NaOCl$.
statements.E: In the preparation of iodoform from ethanol, 3 mol of $I_2$ are consumed per mole of ethanol.

solution.key_concept: This question tests the reaction conditions, separation method and stoichiometry of these preparations.
steps: A is correct.
B is incorrect: the o-isomer stays in the ethanol filtrate and the p-isomer crystallises.
C is correct.
D is correct: $KI$ with $NaOCl$ can replace $I_2$ with $NaOH$.
E is incorrect: $CH_3CH_2OH + 4I_2 + 6NaOH \rightarrow CHI_3 + HCOONa + 5NaI + 5H_2O$ uses 4 mol of $I_2$. The 3 mol figure applies to acetone.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): A, C and D only
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) leaves out D, which is true. Option (2) includes B, which is false. Option (4) includes E, which is false.
solution.common_trap: Using the acetone stoichiometry (3 mol $I_2$) for ethanol, which needs 4 mol because it is first oxidised.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Titrimetric exercises: acids, bases and use of indicators
questions.question: Which indicator is most suitable for titrating acetic acid (a weak acid) against sodium hydroxide solution?

solution.key_concept: For a weak acid against a strong base, the pH jump lies in the basic range, so phenolphthalein (pH 8.2-10) is used.
steps: Acetic acid is a weak acid and $NaOH$ is a strong base.
At the equivalence point the solution is basic, and the steep part of the curve lies above pH 7.
Phenolphthalein changes colour in the range pH 8.2-10, which lies within this jump.
solution.why_not_others: Methyl orange (pH 3.1-4.4) changes colour too early for a weak acid. Either indicator works only for a strong acid with a strong base. No simple indicator works only for a weak acid with a weak base.
solution.common_trap: Assuming that any indicator works for any acid-base titration.
solution.time_saving_tip: Match the indicator to the stronger partner: strong base means phenolphthalein, strong acid means methyl orange.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Titrimetric exercises: acids, bases and use of indicators
questions.question: 1.26 g of oxalic acid dihydrate ($H_2C_2O_4\cdot2H_2O$, molar mass 126 g/mol) is dissolved in water to make 250 mL of solution. 25 mL of this solution requires 20 mL of $NaOH$ solution for complete neutralisation. The molarity of the $NaOH$ solution is

solution.key_concept: At the equivalence point, $n_1M_1V_1 = n_2M_2V_2$. Oxalic acid has n-factor 2 as an acid.
steps: Molarity of oxalic acid: $M = \frac{1.26 \times 1000}{126 \times 250} = 0.04$ M.
Apply $n_1M_1V_1 = n_2M_2V_2$: $2 \times 0.04 \times 25 = 1 \times M \times 20$.
solution.why_not_others: 0.05 M comes from ignoring the n-factor of 2. 0.064 M comes from interchanging the two volumes. 0.14 M comes from using the anhydrous molar mass (90) instead of 126.
solution.common_trap: Forgetting that oxalic acid is dibasic, with n-factor 2.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Titrimetric exercises: acids, bases and use of indicators
questions.question: Ammonium hydroxide solution in a conical flask is titrated with $HCl$ from the burette. Which indicator should be used, and what colour change marks the end point?

solution.key_concept: For a strong acid with a weak base, the pH jump lies in the acidic range, so methyl orange is used. It is yellow in base and red in acid.
steps: $NH_4OH$ is a weak base and $HCl$ is a strong acid, so methyl orange is the correct indicator.
The flask is initially basic, so methyl orange is yellow.
The first slight excess of acid turns it red, so the end point is yellow to red.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): Methyl orange; yellow to red
solution.why_not_others: Phenolphthalein is unsuitable for a strong acid-weak base titration. Red to yellow would be the change when base is added to acid, which is the reverse of this set-up.
solution.common_trap: Choosing phenolphthalein for a strong acid-weak base titration.
solution.time_saving_tip: The colour at the end point is the colour of the indicator in the medium being added from the burette.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Titrimetric exercises: acids, bases and use of indicators
questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: Only a few drops of indicator are added in an acid-base titration.
statements.R: Indicators are strong electrolytes that do not react with the acid or the base being titrated.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: Indicators are themselves weak acids or weak bases, so only a few drops are used to avoid consuming titrant.
steps: In practice only a few drops of indicator are used, so A is true.
Indicators are weak acids or weak bases, not inert strong electrolytes, so R is false.
Because they react with the titrant, a large amount of indicator would introduce an error.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): A is true but R is false
solution.why_not_others: R is false, so options (1) and (2) cannot be correct. A is a correct practical rule, so option (4) is ruled out.
solution.common_trap: Thinking indicators are chemically inert.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Titrimetric exercises: acids, bases and use of indicators
questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: For a strong acid-strong base titration, either phenolphthalein or methyl orange can be used, because the pH jump extends roughly from 3 to 11.
statements.II: Methyl orange (colour change range pH 3.1-4.4) is suitable for titrating a strong acid with a weak base, because the pH jump in this titration lies in the acidic range.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: The indicator's colour-change range must lie within the steep part of the titration curve.
steps: Strong acid-strong base: the jump of about pH 3 to 11 contains both indicator ranges, so Statement I is correct.
Strong acid-weak base: the jump lies in the acidic region, which matches methyl orange (3.1-4.4), so Statement II is correct.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
solution.why_not_others: Both statements agree with the indicator-selection rules, so no option marking either statement as incorrect is valid.
solution.common_trap: Believing that phenolphthalein is the only correct indicator for a strong acid-strong base titration.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Oxalic acid vs KMnO4 and Mohr's salt vs KMnO4
questions.question: Which acid is used to acidify the solution in titrations with $KMnO_4$?

solution.key_concept: Only dilute $H_2SO_4$ is used, because it is neither oxidised by $KMnO_4$ nor an oxidant itself.
steps: $HCl$ is oxidised by $KMnO_4$ to $Cl_2$, which gives high readings.
$HNO_3$ is itself an oxidising agent and interferes with the titration.
Dilute $H_2SO_4$ does neither, so it is used.
solution.why_not_others: $HCl$ consumes $KMnO_4$. Both dilute and concentrated $HNO_3$ act as oxidants.
solution.common_trap: Thinking that any strong acid can be used to acidify $KMnO_4$ titrations.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Oxalic acid vs KMnO4 and Mohr's salt vs KMnO4
questions.question: 20 mL of a 0.1 M $Fe^{2+}$ solution (from Mohr's salt) is titrated in acidic medium with 0.02 M $KMnO_4$. The volume of $KMnO_4$ solution required to reach the end point is

steps: Set up the relation: $5 \times 0.02 \times V = 0.1 \times 20$.
Simplify: $0.1V = 2$.
Solve: $V = 20$ mL.
solution.why_not_others: 100 mL comes from assuming equal moles. 40 mL comes from using the oxalate ratio of 2:5. 500 mL comes from putting the factor 5 on the wrong side.
solution.common_trap: Using a 1:1 mole ratio between $KMnO_4$ and $Fe^{2+}$.
solution.time_saving_tip: Equivalents: $0.1 \times 20 = 2$ meq of $Fe^{2+}$; the normality of $KMnO_4$ is $0.1$ N, so $V = 20$ mL.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Oxalic acid vs KMnO4 and Mohr's salt vs KMnO4
questions.question: 20 mL of 0.05 M oxalic acid is titrated in acidic medium and requires 25 mL of $KMnO_4$ solution to reach the end point. The molarity of the $KMnO_4$ solution is

solution.key_concept: For oxalic acid against $KMnO_4$: $5M_{KMnO_4}V_{KMnO_4} = 2M_{ox}V_{ox}$.
steps: Set up the relation: $5 \times M \times 25 = 2 \times 0.05 \times 20$.
Simplify: $125M = 2$.
Solve: $M = 0.016$ M.
solution.why_not_others: 0.04 M comes from assuming equal moles. 0.10 M comes from interchanging the factors 5 and 2. 0.025 M comes from interchanging the two volumes.
solution.common_trap: Using equal moles of $KMnO_4$ and oxalic acid instead of the 2:5 ratio.

questions.topic: Oxalic acid vs KMnO4 and Mohr's salt vs KMnO4
questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_I.label: A
list_I.text: Equivalent weight of $KMnO_4$ in acid medium

list_I.label: B
list_I.text: n-factor of oxalic acid in its reaction with $KMnO_4$

list_I.label: C
list_I.text: n-factor of $Fe^{2+}$ (Mohr's salt) in its reaction with $KMnO_4$

solution.key_concept: In acid medium, $MnO_4^- \rightarrow Mn^{2+}$ has n-factor 5, so $E = 158/5 = 31.6$. Oxalic acid has n-factor 2 and $Fe^{2+}$ has n-factor 1.
steps: B: $C_2O_4^{2-} \rightarrow 2CO_2$ involves 2 electrons, so B-II.
C: $Fe^{2+} \rightarrow Fe^{3+}$ involves 1 electron, so C-III.
D: $Mn$ changes from +7 to +2, so D-IV.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about redox titrations with $KMnO_4$ are correct?

statements.A: $KMnO_4$ is taken in the burette and the reducing agent in the conical flask.
statements.B: The end point is marked by the first permanent light pink colour.
statements.C: Mohr's salt solution is warmed to 60-70 °C before titration.
statements.E: $Mn^{2+}$ ions formed during the reaction autocatalyse the oxidation of oxalic acid.

options: A, C, D and E only

solution.key_concept: $KMnO_4$ acts as a self-indicator and is not a primary standard. Only oxalic acid is warmed; Mohr's salt is titrated cold.
steps: A is true: $KMnO_4$ goes in the burette.
B is true: $KMnO_4$ is a self-indicator, and the first permanent light pink colour marks the end point.
C is false: heating lets air oxidise $Fe^{2+}$, so Mohr's salt is titrated at room temperature.
D is false: $KMnO_4$ is not available pure and decomposes in light.
E is true: the $Mn^{2+}$ formed autocatalyses the oxalate reaction.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): A, B and E only
solution.why_not_others: Every other option includes C or D, and both of these statements are false.
solution.common_trap: Warming Mohr's salt solution in the same way as oxalic acid.

questions.question: Which reagent gives a rosy-red precipitate with $Ni^{2+}$ ions?

solution.key_concept: $Ni^{2+}$ forms rosy-red nickel dimethylglyoximate, $[Ni(dmg)_2]$.
steps: The reaction is $Ni^{2+} + 2\,dmgH \rightarrow [Ni(dmg)_2] + 2H^+$, which gives a rosy-red precipitate.
solution.why_not_others: Nessler's reagent is the test for $NH_4^+$. $K_4[Fe(CN)_6]$ is used to test for $Fe^{3+}$, $Cu^{2+}$ and $Zn^{2+}$. $KSCN$ gives a blood-red colour with $Fe^{3+}$.
solution.common_trap: Confusing the rosy-red $Ni$-dmg precipitate with the blood-red $Fe$-$SCN$ colour.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Qualitative salt analysis: cations Pb2+, Cu2+, Al3+, Fe3+, Zn2+, Ni2+, Ca2+, Ba2+, Mg2+, NH4+
questions.question: In the precipitation of Group III cations, $NH_4Cl$ is added before $NH_4OH$ in order to
options: suppress the $OH^-$ concentration by the common-ion effect, so that only Group III hydroxides precipitate
increase the $S^{2-}$ concentration, so that Group IV sulphides precipitate
make the solution acidic, so that Group II sulphides precipitate
dissolve $PbCl_2$ left over from Group I

solution.key_concept: $NH_4^+$ from $NH_4Cl$ suppresses the ionisation of $NH_4OH$ by the common-ion effect.
steps: Adding $NH_4Cl$ lowers $[OH^-]$.
Only hydroxides of very low solubility, such as $Fe(OH)_3$ and $Al(OH)_3$, precipitate at this lower $[OH^-]$.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): suppress the $OH^-$ concentration by the common-ion effect, so that only Group III hydroxides precipitate
solution.why_not_others: Raising $[S^{2-}]$ is the role of the ammoniacal medium in Group IV. Acidic medium is used in Group II. $NH_4Cl$ has no role in dissolving $PbCl_2$.
solution.common_trap: Mixing up the roles of the reagents used in Group III and Group IV.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Qualitative salt analysis: cations Pb2+, Cu2+, Al3+, Fe3+, Zn2+, Ni2+, Ca2+, Ba2+, Mg2+, NH4+
questions.question: A salt solution gives a yellow precipitate with $K_2CrO_4$, and the salt imparts an apple-green colour to the flame. The cation present is

solution.key_concept: $Ba^{2+}$ gives yellow $BaCrO_4$ and an apple-green flame.
steps: A yellow chromate precipitate points to either $Ba^{2+}$ or $Pb^{2+}$.
The apple-green flame identifies $Ba^{2+}$.
solution.why_not_others: $Pb^{2+}$ also gives yellow $PbCrO_4$ but not an apple-green flame. $Ca^{2+}$ gives a brick-red flame. $Cu^{2+}$ gives a blue-green flame.
solution.common_trap: Choosing $Pb^{2+}$ on the basis of the yellow chromate alone.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Qualitative salt analysis: cations Pb2+, Cu2+, Al3+, Fe3+, Zn2+, Ni2+, Ca2+, Ba2+, Mg2+, NH4+
questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: When $H_2S$ is passed through a solution acidified with dilute $HCl$, $ZnS$ precipitates along with $CuS$.
statements.R: In the presence of dilute $HCl$, the $S^{2-}$ concentration is low, so only sulphides of very low $K_{sp}$ precipitate.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: Low $[S^{2-}]$ in acid medium precipitates only Group II sulphides; $ZnS$ needs the higher $[S^{2-}]$ of an ammoniacal medium.
steps: R is true: $H^+$ suppresses the ionisation of $H_2S$, which lowers $[S^{2-}]$.
Because of this, only very low $K_{sp}$ sulphides such as $CuS$ precipitate.
$ZnS$ precipitates in Group IV in ammoniacal medium, so A is false.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): A is false but R is true
solution.why_not_others: A is false, so options (1), (2) and (3) are all ruled out.
solution.common_trap: Assuming that all metal sulphides precipitate whenever $H_2S$ is passed.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Qualitative salt analysis: cations Pb2+, Cu2+, Al3+, Fe3+, Zn2+, Ni2+, Ca2+, Ba2+, Mg2+, NH4+
questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: $Pb^{2+}$ can appear in both Group I and Group II, because $PbCl_2$ is only partly insoluble.
statements.II: In Group IV, the ammoniacal medium raises $[S^{2-}]$, so white $ZnS$ and black $NiS$ precipitate.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: $PbCl_2$ is partly soluble, so some $Pb^{2+}$ passes into Group II. Ammoniacal $H_2S$ supplies the higher $[S^{2-}]$ needed for Group IV sulphides.
steps: Statement I: $PbCl_2$ is partly soluble, so leftover $Pb^{2+}$ precipitates in Group II. This is correct.
Statement II: the ammoniacal medium increases $[S^{2-}]$, giving white $ZnS$ and black $NiS$. This is correct.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
solution.why_not_others: Both statements agree with the notes, so no option marking either statement as incorrect is valid.
solution.common_trap: Thinking that $Pb^{2+}$ is removed completely in Group I.

questions.question: A salt gives brisk effervescence with dilute $H_2SO_4$, and the gas evolved turns lime water milky. The gas is

solution.key_concept: A carbonate gives $CO_2$ with dilute $H_2SO_4$, and $CO_2$ turns lime water milky by forming $CaCO_3$.
steps: The gas comes from a carbonate reacting with dilute acid.
Lime water turns milky by the reaction $Ca(OH)_2 + CO_2 \rightarrow CaCO_3 + H_2O$.
solution.why_not_others: $H_2S$ has a rotten-egg smell and blackens lead acetate paper. $NO_2$ appears as brown fumes. $HCl$ needs concentrated $H_2SO_4$ and gives white fumes with $NH_3$.

questions.question: The oxidation state of iron in the brown ring complex $[Fe(H_2O)_5NO]^{2+}$ formed in the nitrate test is

solution.key_concept: In the brown ring complex, NO is present as $NO^+$.
steps: The overall charge is +2. Water is neutral and NO carries +1.
So the oxidation state of iron is $+2 - 1 = +1$.
solution.why_not_others: +2 comes from treating NO as neutral. +3 and 0 have no basis.
solution.common_trap: Assuming iron stays +2 because $FeSO_4$ is used.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Qualitative salt analysis: anions CO3 2-, S2-, SO4 2-, NO3-, NO2-, Cl-, Br-, I-
questions.question: A salt is heated with solid $K_2Cr_2O_7$ and concentrated $H_2SO_4$. Orange-red vapours are evolved, which give a yellow solution when passed into $NaOH$. This solution, acidified with acetic acid, gives a yellow precipitate with lead acetate. The anion present is

solution.key_concept: This is the chromyl chloride test, which only $Cl^-$ gives.
steps: The orange-red vapours are $CrO_2Cl_2$.
In $NaOH$ they form yellow $Na_2CrO_4$, which gives yellow $PbCrO_4$ with lead acetate.
solution.why_not_others: Bromides and iodides do not form $CrO_2X_2$. Nitrate is identified by the brown ring test.
solution.common_trap: Believing that $Br^-$ also gives the chromyl chloride test because of its reddish-brown vapours.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Qualitative salt analysis: anions CO3 2-, S2-, SO4 2-, NO3-, NO2-, Cl-, Br-, I-
questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_II.label: III
list_II.text: White precipitate with $BaCl_2$, insoluble in conc. $HCl$

solution.key_concept: Each anion has its own confirmatory test.
steps: $S^{2-}$ gives a violet colour with sodium nitroprusside, so A-I.
$NO_2^-$ turns $KI$-starch paper blue, so B-II.
$SO_4^{2-}$ gives $BaSO_4$, which is insoluble in conc. acid, so C-III.
$I^-$ releases $I_2$, which gives a violet $CCl_4$ layer, so D-IV.
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) interchanges the two 'violet' tests. Options (2) and (3) misassign the nitrite and sulphate tests.
solution.common_trap: Confusing the violet nitroprusside colour of sulphide with the violet iodine layer.

questions.topic: Qualitative salt analysis: anions CO3 2-, S2-, SO4 2-, NO3-, NO2-, Cl-, Br-, I-
questions.question: Which of the following statements about tests for anions are correct?

statements.B: $AgI$ is yellow and readily soluble in $NH_4OH$.
statements.C: $NO_2^-$ interferes with the brown ring test for nitrate and is removed using sulphamic acid.
statements.D: $Br^-$ gives reddish-brown vapours when heated with concentrated $H_2SO_4$.

options: A, C, D and E only

solution.key_concept: The silver halides differ in solubility in $NH_4OH$, and $BaSO_4$ is insoluble in concentrated acids.
steps: A is true: $AgCl$ is white and dissolves in $NH_4OH$.
B is false: $AgI$ is insoluble in $NH_4OH$.
C is true: sulphamic acid removes interfering nitrite.
D is true: $Br^-$ gives reddish-brown $Br_2$ vapours.
E is false: $BaSO_4$ is insoluble in conc. $HCl$.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): A, C and D only
solution.why_not_others: Every other option includes B or E, and both of these statements are false.
solution.common_trap: Treating all silver halides as soluble in ammonia.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Enthalpy of solution of CuSO4
questions.question: When anhydrous $CuSO_4$ is dissolved in water in a calorimeter, which observation is made?
options: The temperature falls and $\Delta_{sol}H$ is positive
The temperature remains unchanged and $\Delta_{sol}H$ is zero
The temperature rises and $\Delta_{sol}H$ is negative
The temperature falls and $\Delta_{sol}H$ is negative

solution.key_concept: Anhydrous $CuSO_4$ dissolves exothermically, at about $-66.5$ kJ/mol, because its hydration energy outweighs its lattice energy.
steps: In anhydrous $CuSO_4$ the ions are not yet hydrated, so a large hydration energy is released on dissolving.
This energy exceeds the lattice energy, so heat is released and the temperature rises.
A temperature rise means an exothermic process, so $\Delta_{sol}H$ is negative.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): The temperature rises and $\Delta_{sol}H$ is negative
solution.why_not_others: A fall in temperature is seen for $CuSO_4\cdot5H_2O$, not for the anhydrous salt. The temperature does change, so $\Delta H$ is not zero. A fall in temperature cannot go with a negative $\Delta H$.
solution.common_trap: Confusing the anhydrous salt (exothermic) with the blue pentahydrate (slightly endothermic).
solution.time_saving_tip: White anhydrous salt gives heat; blue hydrated salt absorbs heat.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Enthalpy of solution of CuSO4
questions.question: 15.95 g of anhydrous $CuSO_4$ (molar mass 159.5 g/mol) is dissolved in 180 g of water in a calorimeter of water equivalent 20 g. The temperature rises by 8.0 K. Take the specific heat as 4.18 J g$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$, and take the heat-absorbing mass as the water plus the water equivalent of the calorimeter. What is the molar enthalpy of solution of anhydrous $CuSO_4$?

solution.key_concept: $q = (m + W)\,s\,\Delta T$ and $\Delta_{sol}H = -\frac{q \times M}{w}$, with the sign set by the temperature change.
steps: The temperature rose, so the process is exothermic and $\Delta_{sol}H = -66.9$ kJ/mol.
solution.why_not_others: $+66.9$ has the wrong sign for a temperature rise. $-60.2$ comes from ignoring the water equivalent and using only 180 g. $-6.69$ is the heat for 0.1 mol, not per mole.
solution.common_trap: Leaving out the water equivalent of the calorimeter, or forgetting to convert to a per-mole value.
solution.time_saving_tip: The answer should be close to the known value of about $-66.5$ kJ/mol.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Enthalpy of solution of CuSO4
questions.question: The enthalpy of solution of anhydrous $CuSO_4$ is $-66.5$ kJ/mol and that of $CuSO_4\cdot5H_2O$ is $+11.7$ kJ/mol. What is the enthalpy change for $CuSO_4(s) + 5H_2O(l) \rightarrow CuSO_4\cdot5H_2O(s)$?

solution.key_concept: Hess's law gives $\Delta_{hyd}H = \Delta_{sol}H(anhydrous) - \Delta_{sol}H(hydrated)$.
steps: Anhydrous salt to solution: $-66.5$ kJ. Hydrated salt to solution: $+11.7$ kJ.
Anhydrous salt to hydrated salt = (anhydrous to solution) minus (hydrated to solution).
solution.why_not_others: $-54.8$ comes from adding the two values instead of subtracting. $+78.2$ reverses the order of subtraction. $+54.8$ combines both errors.
solution.common_trap: Adding the two enthalpies of solution, or subtracting them in the wrong order.
solution.time_saving_tip: Hydration of the anhydrous salt releases heat, so the answer must be negative and larger in magnitude than 66.5.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Enthalpy of solution of CuSO4
questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: Dissolution of $CuSO_4\cdot5H_2O$ in water in a calorimeter is accompanied by a fall in temperature.
statements.R: For $CuSO_4\cdot5H_2O$, the hydration energy released on dissolving far exceeds its lattice energy.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: $CuSO_4\cdot5H_2O$ dissolves slightly endothermically (about $+11.7$ kJ/mol) because its ions are already partly hydrated.
steps: The pentahydrate absorbs heat on dissolving, so the temperature falls. A is true.
Its ions are already partly hydrated, so little extra hydration energy is released.
If hydration energy far exceeded lattice energy, the process would be exothermic, so R is false. R actually describes anhydrous $CuSO_4$.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): A is true but R is false
solution.why_not_others: R is false, so the options in which both statements are true are ruled out. A is true, so 'A is false but R is true' is also wrong.
solution.common_trap: Applying the reasoning for the anhydrous salt to the pentahydrate.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Enthalpy of solution of CuSO4
questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: Anhydrous $CuSO_4$ dissolves exothermically because its lattice energy is greater than its hydration energy.
statements.II: The enthalpy of hydration of $CuSO_4$ to $CuSO_4\cdot5H_2O$ is obtained by subtracting the enthalpy of solution of the pentahydrate from that of the anhydrous salt.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: Dissolution is exothermic when hydration energy outweighs lattice energy. Hess's law gives $\Delta_{hyd}H = \Delta_{sol}H(anhydrous) - \Delta_{sol}H(hydrated)$.
steps: Anhydrous $CuSO_4$ is exothermic on dissolving because the large hydration energy outweighs the lattice energy. Statement I reverses this, so it is incorrect.
$\Delta_{hyd}H = \Delta_{sol}H(anhydrous) - \Delta_{sol}H(hydrated) = -66.5 - 11.7 = -78.2$ kJ/mol, so Statement II is correct.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
solution.why_not_others: Statement I gives the wrong reason for the heat release, so any option calling it correct fails. Statement II is a direct application of Hess's law, so it cannot be called incorrect.
solution.common_trap: Accepting Statement I because its conclusion (exothermic) is right, without checking its reasoning.
solution.time_saving_tip: Heat is released only when more energy is gained on hydration than is spent breaking the lattice.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Enthalpy of neutralization of a strong acid and a strong base
questions.question: The enthalpy of neutralisation of dilute $HNO_3$ with dilute $KOH$ is approximately

solution.key_concept: For any strong acid with any strong base, the only net reaction is $H^+ + OH^- \rightarrow H_2O$, with $\Delta H \approx -57.1$ kJ/mol.
steps: $HNO_3$ and $KOH$ are both strong and fully ionised.
The net reaction is $H^+(aq) + OH^-(aq) \rightarrow H_2O(l)$.
So $\Delta_{neut}H \approx -57.1$ kJ/mol.
solution.why_not_others: 13.7 is the value in kcal, not kJ. Neutralisation is exothermic, so $+57.1$ is wrong. $-114.2$ would be the heat for 2 mol of water.
solution.common_trap: Mixing up the kJ and kcal values, or taking the sign as positive.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Enthalpy of neutralization of a strong acid and a strong base
questions.question: 100 mL of 0.5 M $HCl$ and 100 mL of 0.5 M $NaOH$, both at the same initial temperature, are mixed in a calorimeter of negligible water equivalent. The temperature rises by 3.4 K. Taking the density as 1 g/mL and the specific heat as 4.18 J g$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$, what is the enthalpy of neutralisation?

solution.key_concept: $\Delta_{neut}H = -\frac{(m + W)\,s\,\Delta T}{n_{H_2O}}$
steps: Total mass $= 200$ g and $W = 0$.
$\Delta_{neut}H = -2842.4/0.05 = -56848$ J/mol $\approx -56.8$ kJ/mol.
solution.why_not_others: $-28.4$ comes from using the mass of only one solution (100 g). $+56.8$ has the wrong sign for a temperature rise. $-2.84$ is the total heat in kJ, not divided by the moles of water.
solution.common_trap: Using the volume of only one solution as the mass that absorbs heat.
solution.time_saving_tip: For a strong acid with a strong base the answer must be close to $-57.1$ kJ/mol.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Enthalpy of neutralization of a strong acid and a strong base
questions.question: 200 mL of 0.5 M $HCl$ is mixed with 100 mL of 0.5 M $NaOH$. Taking $\Delta_{neut}H = -57.1$ kJ/mol, what is the amount of heat released?

solution.key_concept: The heat released depends on the moles of water formed, which are set by the limiting reagent.
steps: Moles of $HCl = 0.200 \times 0.5 = 0.10$ mol.
Moles of $NaOH = 0.100 \times 0.5 = 0.05$ mol, so $NaOH$ is limiting.
Moles of water formed $= 0.05$ mol.
Heat released $= 0.05 \times 57.1 = 2.855 \approx 2.86$ kJ.
solution.why_not_others: 5.71 kJ uses the moles of $HCl$, the excess reagent. 8.57 kJ adds the moles of acid and base. 1.43 kJ wrongly halves the moles of the limiting reagent.
solution.common_trap: Basing the heat on the reagent in excess instead of the limiting reagent.
solution.time_saving_tip: Find the smaller number of moles first; only that amount reacts.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Enthalpy of neutralization of a strong acid and a strong base
questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_II.label: I
list_II.text: About $-57.1$ kJ/mol, since both are fully ionised

list_II.label: II
list_II.text: Magnitude less than 57.1 kJ/mol, as energy is spent ionising the weak acid

list_II.label: III
list_II.text: Magnitude more than 57.1 kJ/mol, due to the high hydration enthalpy of the anion

list_II.label: IV
list_II.text: Magnitude less than 57.1 kJ/mol, as energy is spent ionising the weak base

solution.key_concept: The value is about $-57.1$ kJ/mol for a strong acid with a strong base. It is smaller in magnitude with a weak electrolyte, and larger for $HF$ because $F^-$ is strongly hydrated.
steps: $HCl$ + $NaOH$: strong acid with strong base, so I.
$CH_3COOH$ is a weak acid, so II.
$HF$: the high hydration enthalpy of $F^-$ makes the magnitude exceed 57.1, so III.
$NH_4OH$ is a weak base, so IV.
solution.why_not_others: Option 1 swaps the weak acid and the weak base. Option 2 puts $HF$ at the standard value. Option 4 gives acetic acid the standard value.
solution.common_trap: Treating $HF$ like other weak acids, whose magnitude is smaller than 57.1 kJ/mol.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Enthalpy of neutralization of a strong acid and a strong base
questions.question: Which of the following statements about enthalpy of neutralisation are correct?

statements.A: The enthalpy of neutralisation of $H_2SO_4$ with $NaOH$, per g-equivalent, is about $-57.1$ kJ/mol.
statements.B: The acid and base solutions must be at the same initial temperature before mixing.
statements.C: For $CH_3COOH$ with $NaOH$ the value is $-57.1$ kJ/mol, because the acid is eventually neutralised completely.
statements.D: If the enthalpy of ionisation of a weak acid is 2.1 kJ/mol, the magnitude of its enthalpy of neutralisation with a strong base is 55.0 kJ/mol.
statements.E: The heat released depends on the moles of water formed, which are fixed by the reagent present in excess.

solution.key_concept: The value is about $-57.1$ kJ/mol per g-equivalent for strong acids and bases. $|\Delta_{neut}H_{weak}| = 57.1 - \Delta_{ion}H$, and the limiting reagent fixes the heat released.
steps: A: both are strong, and the value is per g-equivalent, so it is $-57.1$ kJ/mol. Correct.
B: equal initial temperatures are required. Correct.
C: part of the heat is used to ionise acetic acid, so the magnitude is smaller. Incorrect.
D: $57.1 - 2.1 = 55.0$ kJ/mol. Correct.
E: the limiting reagent, not the excess one, fixes the moles of water. Incorrect.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): A, B and D only
solution.why_not_others: Option 1 leaves out the correct statement D. Option 2 includes the incorrect statement C. Option 3 includes the incorrect statement E and leaves out B.
solution.common_trap: Taking $\Delta_{neut}H$ of acetic acid with $NaOH$ as $-57.1$ kJ/mol.
solution.time_saving_tip: Rule out C and E first; only one option then remains.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Preparation of lyophilic and lyophobic sols
questions.question: Which of the following is a lyophilic sol?

solution.key_concept: Lyophilic sols, such as those of starch, gum, gelatin and egg albumin, are made directly by warming the substance with water.
steps: Starch forms a sol when its cold-water paste is poured into boiling water.
This sol is reversible and self-stabilised by solvation, so it is lyophilic.
solution.why_not_others: $Fe(OH)_3$, $As_2S_3$ and $Al(OH)_3$ sols are lyophobic. They need special methods of preparation and a stabilising ion.
solution.common_trap: Thinking that any sol prepared using water is lyophilic.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Preparation of lyophilic and lyophobic sols
questions.question: A ferric hydroxide sol is correctly prepared by
options: passing $H_2S$ into a dilute solution of $FeCl_3$
warming solid $Fe(OH)_3$ directly with water, as is done for gelatin
adding $FeCl_3$ solution dropwise to boiling water

solution.key_concept: $Fe(OH)_3$ sol is formed by hydrolysis: $FeCl_3 + 3H_2O \xrightarrow{boil} Fe(OH)_3(sol) + 3HCl$.
steps: Hydrolysis of $FeCl_3$ requires boiling water.
$FeCl_3$ solution is added dropwise to boiling water, giving a red-brown, positively charged sol.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): adding $FeCl_3$ solution dropwise to boiling water
solution.why_not_others: Passing $H_2S$ is the double decomposition method used for $As_2S_3$ sol, starting from $As_2O_3$. Cold water does not give the sol. Direct warming with water works only for lyophilic substances.
solution.common_trap: Using cold water instead of boiling water.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Preparation of lyophilic and lyophobic sols
questions.question: Arsenious sulphide sol is prepared by passing $H_2S$ into a dilute solution of $As_2O_3$. Which electrolyte, at equal molar concentration, will coagulate this sol most effectively?

solution.key_concept: By the Hardy-Schulze rule, the higher the charge of the oppositely charged ion, the greater its coagulating power.
steps: $As_2S_3$ sol is negatively charged because it adsorbs $S^{2-}$.
So the cations are the coagulating ions.
Among $Na^+$, $Ba^{2+}$ and $Al^{3+}$, the ion $Al^{3+}$ has the highest charge, so $AlCl_3$ is most effective.
solution.why_not_others: $Na_3PO_4$ has a highly charged anion, but anions do not coagulate a negative sol; its cation is only $Na^+$. $NaCl$ ($Na^+$) and $BaCl_2$ ($Ba^{2+}$) have cations of lower charge.
solution.common_trap: Choosing $Na_3PO_4$ because of $PO_4^{3-}$, forgetting that $As_2S_3$ sol is negative.
solution.time_saving_tip: Find the charge on the sol first, then look for the most highly charged opposite ion.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Preparation of lyophilic and lyophobic sols
questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: Ferric hydroxide sol is prepared by adding $FeCl_3$ solution to cold water.
statements.R: Ferric hydroxide sol is formed by the hydrolysis of $FeCl_3$.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: $FeCl_3 + 3H_2O \xrightarrow{boil} Fe(OH)_3(sol) + 3HCl$ requires boiling water.
steps: $FeCl_3$ is added to boiling water, not cold water, so A is false.
The sol does form by hydrolysis of $FeCl_3$, so R is true.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): A is false but R is true
solution.why_not_others: A is false, so every option that calls A true is ruled out.
solution.common_trap: Overlooking the boiling-water condition.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Preparation of lyophilic and lyophobic sols
questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: Excess electrolyte in a freshly prepared ferric hydroxide sol is removed by dialysis, since it would otherwise coagulate the sol.
statements.II: Lyophilic sols such as gelatin sol are stabilised only by the charge on their particles, and are therefore easily coagulated by small amounts of electrolyte.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: Lyophobic sols are stabilised only by charge and need dialysis. Lyophilic sols are self-stabilised by solvation and are not easily coagulated.
steps: Dialysis removes excess electrolyte, which would otherwise coagulate a lyophobic sol. Statement I is correct.
Gelatin sol is lyophilic, so it is stabilised by solvation and is highly stable. Statement II is incorrect.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
solution.why_not_others: Statement II describes lyophobic sols, not lyophilic ones, so any option calling it correct fails. Statement I is directly supported by the notes.
solution.common_trap: Attributing the charge-only stabilisation of lyophobic sols to lyophilic sols.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Kinetic study of the reaction of iodide ions with hydrogen peroxide
questions.question: In the iodine clock study of the reaction between $H_2O_2$ and $I^-$ in acid medium, what is the role of the small fixed amount of $Na_2S_2O_3$ added?
options: It reduces the $I_2$ formed back to $I^-$, keeping $[I^-]$ effectively constant and acting as a clock
It gives the blue colour that marks the end of the timed interval
It supplies the $H^+$ ions needed for the reaction

solution.key_concept: Thiosulphate reacts as $I_2 + 2S_2O_3^{2-} \rightarrow 2I^- + S_4O_6^{2-}$, so it is both the clock and the source that regenerates $I^-$.
steps: The $I_2$ formed is immediately reduced back to $I^-$ by thiosulphate.
This keeps the solution colourless and $[I^-]$ effectively constant.
When the thiosulphate is used up, free $I_2$ appears and the blue colour develops.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): It reduces the $I_2$ formed back to $I^-$, keeping $[I^-]$ effectively constant and acting as a clock
solution.why_not_others: $H_2O_2$, not thiosulphate, oxidises $I^-$. Starch, not thiosulphate, gives the blue colour. Thiosulphate does not supply $H^+$.
solution.common_trap: Confusing the role of thiosulphate with that of the starch indicator.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Kinetic study of the reaction of iodide ions with hydrogen peroxide
questions.question: In an iodine clock experiment on the reaction $H_2O_2 + 2I^- + 2H^+ \rightarrow I_2 + 2H_2O$, the blue colour appears after 120 s. The experiment is repeated with $[H_2O_2]$ doubled and $[I^-]$ tripled, with everything else unchanged. After how long will the blue colour appear?

solution.key_concept: Rate $= k[H_2O_2][I^-]$ and rate $\propto \frac{1}{t}$.
steps: The new rate is $2 \times 3 = 6$ times the original rate.
Time is inversely proportional to rate, so $t = 120/6 = 20$ s.
solution.why_not_others: 720 s comes from multiplying the time instead of dividing. 40 s accounts only for the change in $[I^-]$, and 60 s only for the change in $[H_2O_2]$.
solution.common_trap: Treating time as directly proportional to rate.
solution.time_saving_tip: Multiply the concentration factors to get the rate factor, then divide the time by it.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Kinetic study of the reaction of iodide ions with hydrogen peroxide
questions.question: For the reaction of $H_2O_2$ with $I^-$ in acid medium, $k = 0.02$ L mol$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$. What is the rate when $[H_2O_2] = 0.10$ M, $[I^-] = 0.05$ M and $[H^+] = 0.5$ M?

solution.key_concept: The experimental rate law is rate $= k[H_2O_2][I^-]$, which is second order overall. It does not follow the stoichiometry of the balanced equation.
steps: Rate $= 0.02 \times 0.10 \times 0.05$.
$[H^+]$ does not appear in the rate law, and $[I^-]$ is raised to the first power.
solution.why_not_others: $5.0\times10^{-6}$ squares $[I^-]$ according to the stoichiometry. $2.0\times10^{-3}$ leaves out $[I^-]$. $5.0\times10^{-5}$ wrongly includes $[H^+]$.
solution.common_trap: Writing the rate law from the coefficients of the balanced equation.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Kinetic study of the reaction of iodide ions with hydrogen peroxide
questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_I.label: C
list_I.text: Time $t$ for the blue colour to appear

list_II.label: I
list_II.text: Gives a blue colour with free $I_2$

list_II.label: III
list_II.text: Shortens the time for the blue colour, consistent with the Arrhenius equation

solution.key_concept: In the clock set-up, thiosulphate consumes $I_2$, starch signals free $I_2$, rate $\propto \frac{1}{t}$, and a higher temperature gives a faster rate.
steps: Thiosulphate reduces $I_2$ to $I^-$, so A-II.
Starch gives a blue colour with $I_2$, so B-I.
Rate $\propto 1/t$, so C-IV.
A higher temperature gives a shorter time, so D-III.
solution.why_not_others: Option 1 swaps the roles of thiosulphate and starch. Option 3 swaps C and D. Option 4 swaps A and C.
solution.common_trap: Swapping the roles of the clock reagent and the indicator.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.topic: Kinetic study of the reaction of iodide ions with hydrogen peroxide
questions.question: Which of the following statements about the kinetic study of the reaction of $I^-$ with $H_2O_2$ are correct?

statements.A: The rate law is rate $= k[H_2O_2][I^-]^2[H^+]^2$, as given by the balanced equation.
statements.B: The reaction is second order overall.
statements.C: Thiosulphate regenerates $I^-$, so $[I^-]$ remains effectively constant during the timed interval.
statements.D: Doubling $[I^-]$ while keeping $[H_2O_2]$ constant doubles the time for the blue colour to appear.
statements.E: The blue colour appears only after all the added thiosulphate has been consumed.

solution.key_concept: Rate $= k[H_2O_2][I^-]$ (overall second order), rate $\propto 1/t$, and thiosulphate acts as the clock.
steps: A: the experimental rate law is first order in each reactant, not stoichiometric. Incorrect.
B: $1 + 1 = 2$. Correct.
C: thiosulphate converts $I_2$ back to $I^-$. Correct.
D: doubling $[I^-]$ doubles the rate, so it halves $t$. Incorrect.
E: free $I_2$ appears only after the thiosulphate is used up. Correct.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): B, C and E only
solution.why_not_others: Options 1, 2 and 3 each include A or D, which are incorrect.
solution.common_trap: Assuming that a higher rate means a longer time, or using stoichiometric coefficients as the orders.
solution.time_saving_tip: Rule out A and D; only one option contains neither.
